Relentless Scammers

By: Eugene Botha | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
........the scammers that just would not quit

Unique Selling Point:
A scam that the public should be aware of and be on the lookout for.

Summary:
A group of sophisticated scammers (which includes people from law firms) are using the pretence of high profits on the Luno crypto platform to swindle people out of hundreds of thousands of rand. It is not a crypto scam at all, since no crypto currencies are actually bought as in our previous shows. Money is paid over and is then transferred to several other accounts which make it hard for even banks to recover. And then the scammers return and offer the victims a chance to get the money back – for another payment. Then they pretend they are from the Fraud Department of South Africaan o that recovers stolen money and for a percentage they claimed they can get the money back – the percentage paid up front, of course. And then they illegally withdraw money from the victims account in the night. They just do not give up!

Further information:
When she was approached through a Whatsapp message to make some extra money, it was a God-send for Mrs Viegas, a 65-year old woman from Johannesburg.

She suffers from chronic illnesses, including multiple sclerosis, and some extra funds could be used to address some of the most pressing needs she had. She had some savings, which was her sole source of income. She is a disability pensioner living on a very tight budget and had to be very careful with her spending.

The offer of using some of her money to make a lot more was more than attractive, and she had heard of people earning fabulous amounts of money with crypto currencies.

She was approached through WhatsApp by the CEO of a company referred to as Falcon Xchange, allegedly working in association with Luno, the crypto currency trading platform.

She was invited to utilize an investment opportunity which could provide her with huge returns on her money, much better than any normal investment.

Luno is South Africa’s biggest crypto currency platform and has an excellent track record.

The people contacting her offered to create an account for her on the Falcon Xchange website and manage her portfolio. All she had to do was click on a link, fill in her details and she was set to earn substantial and quick profits on her trading account.
She was advised to pay money into a Standard Bank account and paid over a total amount of R533, 850.00
She then started to receive screen shots of her growing investment account, which soon was in the range of six million rand. It all seemed very legit and the “proof” kept on coming.
After a few weeks on record breaking gains, she decided to withdraw some of the profits and requested pay-outs. This never happened.
Falcon Exchange started to request various fees in order for the funds to be released. These included consultation fees, registration and verification fees, signal fees, cost of transfer fees, activation fees, and so on.
She insisted that they pay back her money and they sent her proof of payment from a Capitec account. The PoP was falsified and the money never arrived.
Mrs Viegas quickly realised that what she believed was an investment scheme was in fact a fraudulent scam.
She went to the Police and was awarded a case number. She contacted Standard Bank who attended to an internal investigation, because she initially paid the money into a Standard Bank account. Standard Bank advised that the money was transferred out of that count to a Capitec and FNB account.
Mrs Viegas was advised by Standard Bank to get a court order to freeze the accounts, and for any available funds to be repatriated to her bank account.
She then approached the law firm Maher Attorneys Incorporated and instructed two up and coming lawyers Mikayla Maher of Maher Attorneys Inc working in association with Gabriela Narotzky of Taitz & Skikne Attorneys. They succeed with a court application late in December 2021 to ensure the funds remained frozen and that the frozen funds or any funds recoverable from the banks would be transferred to Mrs Viegas’s account.
Gabriela and Mikayla have been assisting Mrs Viegas ever since and they have determined the following:
• The Standard Bank account belonged to a Mr Moosa DHlamini, a marketing intern at a reputable law firm. He received the money and paid it into an FNB and Capitec account. The court application was sent to Mr Dhlamini and to his law firm, and he has subsequently been suspended. Another account used was that of a Charmaine Ruud based at a law firm in the Eastern Cape. The attorneys have spoken to both of the these individuals and they claim they merely received money and then transferred it along to an FNB account..
• The FNB account purportedly belongs to a Mr Charles Davids. FNB has advised that there are no longer funds recoverable from this account.
• The “CEO” of Falcon Xchange, who goes by the name KELVIN, (surname unknown), had his number traced on True Caller, with the number registered under the name “New Coin” – another potential cryptocurrency scam being operated by the same group.
The police are investigating, and a docket has been opened. But not much more.
But the saga continues!
• In an unbelievable twist the same fraudsters then attempted to gain further funds from Mrs Viegas by claiming that they could refund all her money back however they would charge a fee of R10 000,00 for their assistance in claiming all her lost money back (as reflected on the Capitec Bank proof of payment).
• But that was still not the end! Mrs Viegas was contacted via Whatsapp by an individual purporting to be from the Fraud Department of South Africa. The individual in question claimed that he would assist Mrs Viegas in obtaining her lost funds and would ensure she is refunded. The individual would simply require 20% of the total moneys recovered. This 20% had to be paid upfront prior to his investigation of the fraud and recoveries of the money. This was an example of yet another attempt and defrauding Mrs Viegas.
• Mrs Viegas continues to receive Whatsapp messages

Gabriela and Mikayla have taken Mrs Viegas under their wing and are still assisting her.
The banks and Luno have been very helpful in the case, although they say as crypto is still unregulated in South Africa, there is little they can do to assist.

The scam is ongoing and on one of the lawyers, Gabriela also received a Whatsapp invitation to the scam.
The two lawyers say the scam in widespread and they want to bring the case to the public’s attention to warn vulnerable groups such as the elderly of the scam and how it works.
Further, a new development in insurance is that there is now specialized insurance cover for instances of fraud, even in instances such as in Mrs Viegas case, where the transactions were authorised and only then found to be fraudulent.
We propose that we expose the scam and confront the scammers whose whereabouts and telephone numbers are known to us.
We have access to:
• All Whatapp messages
• Bank documents
• Copies of the “investment account”
• Court documents
• Telephone numbers of the scammers we know of and new telephone numbers of new Whatsapp approaches.
Interviewees from the following:
• Mrs Viegas
• Gabriela and Mikayla who worked together in association;
• We have the telephone numbers of some of the scammers and the attorneys actually have had conversations with them. We can confront them.
• Sean Andrews on the insurance cover available to individuals and businesses;

Script:


ANA:
If you can invest five hundred thousand, you will have one point seven million rand within two weeks

Derek:
Two weeks.

ANA:
Two weeks.
V/O:
This offer was made to pensioner, Ana Paula Viegas towards the end of last year. It set in motion an extraordinary sequence of intimidation, manipulation, and verbal abuse by a ruthless online syndicate; hell bent on emptying her bank account.

And our investigation of this heartless crime would eventually lead us to a member of the syndicate. A rare face- to face encounter in a usually faceless scam.
V/O:
Ana’s ordeal began with a series of unusual WhatsApp messages. While reading them, a mysterious website for a crypto investment company called Falcon Xchange appeared, promising massive investment returns.

Ana was enticed, filling in an online form asking for her contact details.

At around midnight, her phone rang. Identifying himself as Kelvin, the caller claimed to be the CEO of Falcon Xchange. He said he could make her a very rich woman.
Derek:
Didn’t it sound suspicious?

Ana:
It did sound suspicious, and I questioned. I said… We spoke on the phone for over and hour longer than an hour and you know I actually thought Kelvin was an honest person.
V/O:
But, far from honest, Kelvin was a smooth-talking swindler and Ana the ideal target: elderly, not tech savvy and because of a debilitating condition – vulnerable, too.
Ana:
I was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, and I went on disability pension.
V/O:
The condition not only impacts her physically, but also affects her cognitive abilities.
Ana:
I don’t remember very well because of my MS. I actually jot down everything and sometimes my words that I want to get out normally don’t come out as easy as I want.
V/O:
At the time of Kelvin’s call, Ana had just sold a modest property. It was her nest egg to cover ever increasing medical bills.

Small wonder Kelvin’s late-night promises of huge and almost immediate returns sounded so enticing. (PAUSE) Ana transferred seventy-one thousand rand.
Derek upsound:
Seventy-one thousand invested.

Ana:
That’s right.
V/O:
But that would not end Ana’s ordeal. The fraudsters – with Kelvin at the helm - came back for more.

It was like a circling of sharks and, eventually, Ana got help from two intrepid attorneys: Gabriela Narotzky and Michayla Maher who combed through the evidence.

Shortly after her first payment Ana had received a screenshot of a crypto wallet in her name. It was cleverly designed to make her believe she was onto something big.
Gabriela:
On the left-hand corner there was a mining deposit of seventy-one thousand, and there were profits which showed that she had one million and ten thousand rand.
V/O:
An incredible return within a single day. We asked Peter Fryer, a digital forensics expert to look into the company. His verdict? No such company has ever existed. It is nothing more than an anonymous façade. And it is impossible to trace the website’s owners.
Peter:
What we did manage to determine is that the website is using a virtual address based in Iceland and I do believe that the scammers in this particular scam are an international crime syndicate working outside the borders of South Africa.
V/O:
So, the screenshot Ana received was fake - no real wallet and no real profits. Everything was a lie. Ana was the latest in a long line of phishing scam casualties.

According to the cyber-security provider, Surfshark, South Africa ranks 6th on a list of global cybercrime victims. And phishing – how the banks classified Ana’s case - continues to be the most common. Most victims are 60 or older.

And in Ana’s case , the fraudsters clearly knew they’d stumbled upon the ideal victim. Kelvin messaged her day and night, creating a sense of urgency, pressing her to pay over more money.
Mikayla:
If you do not act now, you will lose out on this opportunity. Make these decisions now. Without really stopping to think or rationalize what you are doing. You’ve got to make these payments. That is really what they did.

I have reams of correspondence here messaging her at one in the morning saying, ”Why are you asleep. Wake up. Make this transaction. Make a payment now. Now is the time. If you don’t do it you are going to lose out. And that really reels the victim in and makes them make decisions they would not necessarily normally do”
V/O:
The relentless intimidation worked. After a few days of bare-faced harassment, Ana was coerced into paying over another four hundred thousand rand. And, to keep her pliant, another fake wallet statement followed – this time showing five point six million rand in profits.
Derek:
And the vulnerable believe this.

Gabriela:
And the vulnerable believe this. A lady at that age or somebody in their 50s or 60s, who are not tech savvy, immediately fall victim to these scams.
V/O:
Then, when Ana tried withdrawing some of the alleged profits, the scammers first demanded sixty-five thousand rand for all manner of fake charges including lost login details and a so-called “signal fee”

By now, Ana had already paid more than five hundred thousand rand to the scammers, without a single pay-out in return. Finally realising she’d been scammed, she went to the Police and Standard Bank and approached Gabriela and Mikayla for help.

With the assistance of all the banks involved, several suspect accounts were frozen, and the lawyers painstakingly pieced together the money trail.
Mikayla:
Monies were paid from Ana’s Standard Bank account into another Standard Bank account and then that money moved to Capitec to FNB and then from FNB to Tyme Bank to Capitec to Standard Bank. It just continually would move until such point that you cannot track it any more or the monies have just been withdrawn.
V/O:
Fryer says this is how syndicates launder money. They often have dozens of accounts, all in other people’s names.
Peter:
It is very common. It is typically a scenario that you would refer to as an e-mule where and individual is paid to open a legit bank account using their own FICA documentation, and once that bank account has been opened, they hand over the bank card with its pin to the syndicate members.
V/O:
This enables them to quickly move illicit funds around, and to withdraw cash at ATMs.

To their surprise Gabriela and Mikayla found that not all the fraudulent accounts had been emptied.
Link:
They then filed an urgent application in the Gauteng North High Court to freeze the various accounts and have what was left in them, repaid to Mrs Viegas.
V/O:
They were able to recover a little over one hundred thousand rand.

But who are these heartless scammers?
LINK:
When we looked at her Whatsapp records and the various bank accounts used to syphon off the money we identified at least 5 role players who are part of the scam.
V/O:
All five of these mystery individuals had contacted Ana at some stage, and we had their numbers. We tried calling them, but unsurprisingly four of them had been disconnected. Then came the fifth, belonging to a Moosa Dhlamini to whom Ana had made most of her payments.
Phone ringing

Moosa:
Hallo.

Derek:
Is that Moosa?

Moosa:
Yes.

Derek:
Moosa Dlamini how are you? It is Derek Watts from Carte Blanche. We would like to talk about your involvement in an alleged scam involving Anna Viegas.

Moosa:
No problem. No problem.
V/O:
We arranged a meeting.
Derek:
Thanks for coming to speak to us all the way from Lens.

Moosa:
Thank you. I want my name to be cleared. I am not a criminal.
V/O:
Far from a cybercrime lynchpin, Moosa claimed to be another of the syndicate’s unsuspecting victims. His only crime? Believing in something too good to be true.
Moosa:
So, I was looking for something to generate income for myself and my family. So I went on Facebook, I went on Instagram, social media platforms typing in the search “How to make online money.” So I get recruited by these Falcon people. They said: Listen, we will offer you a job. We just need your services. They will send money though my account and I was to disperse the money. I was given an FNB account to transfer all the money to.

Derek:
That is the key. They wanted to use your account. What would you get in return?

Moosa:
I would get a percentage
V/O:
According to Moosa, he only discovered his role in the scam when his bank account was frozen after Ana reported the fraud.
Derek:
Did you know that Mrs Viegas was elderly and needed money to pay medical bills?

Moosa:
No, I had no idea. I was not permitted to know the details of the clients.
V/O:
Moosa claims not to have received a cent of what he was promised, and that the people who recruited him have now vanished.

With one scammer’s identity known, we approached the Police for an update on Ana’s case. Their only comment was to confirm that the investigation was still ongoing.

While acknowledging she was fortunate to get even some of her money back, the saga has left Ana devastated, both emotionally and financially.
Derek:
Really you lost half a million.

Ana:
That’s right.

Derek:
How’s that affected you?

Ana:
It has affected me very badly, I am living out of my old age pension.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

PROMO 11”
Accepting a late-night call from a complete stranger. A promise of untold profits.
A pensioner’s dream turned into a nightmare by ruthless scammers. (11)

PROMO 21”
ANA:
If you can invest five hundred thousand, you will have one point seven million rand within two weeks. (10)

A call from a complete stranger led to a loss of over half a million rand. The offer was really too good to be true. (10)



PROMO 21”
A WhatsApp offer on a pensioner’s cell phone was too good to ignore. (6)

ANA:
If you can invest five hundred thousand, you will have one point seven million rand within two weeks. (10)

An opportunity if a lifetime turned into a nightmare of epic proportions. (5)

Shortly after her first payment Ana had received a screenshot of a crypto wallet in her name. It was cleverly designed to make her believe she was onto something big. Gabriela: On the left-hand corner there was a mining deposit of seventy-one thousand, and there were profits which showed that she had one million and ten thousand rand. V/O: An incredible return within a single day. We asked Peter Fryer, a digital forensics expert to look into the company. His verdict? No such company has ever existed. It is nothing more than an anonymous façade. And it is impossible to trace the website’s owners. Peter: What we did manage to determine is that the website is using a virtual address based in Iceland and I do believe that the scammers in this particular scam are an international crime syndicate working outside the borders of South Africa. V/O: So, the screenshot Ana received was fake - no real wallet and no real profits. Everything was a lie. Ana was the latest in a long line of phishing scam casualties. According to the cyber-security provider, Surfshark, South Africa ranks 6th on a list of global cybercrime victims. And phishing – how the banks classified Ana’s case - continues to be the most common. Most victims are 60 or older. And in Ana’s case , the fraudsters clearly knew they’d stumbled upon the ideal victim. Kelvin messaged her day and night, creating a sense of urgency, pressing her to pay over more money. Mikayla: If you do not act now, you will lose out on this opportunity. Make these decisions now. Without really stopping to think or rationalize what you are doing. You’ve got to make these payments. That is really what they did. I have reams of correspondence here messaging her at one in the morning saying, ”Why are you asleep. Wake up. Make this transaction. Make a payment now. Now is the time. If you don’t do it you are going to lose out. And that really reels the victim in and makes them make decisions they would not necessarily normally do” V/O: The relentless intimidation worked. After a few days of bare-faced harassment, Ana was coerced into paying over another four hundred thousand rand. And, to keep her pliant, another fake wallet statement followed – this time showing five point six million rand in profits. Derek: And the vulnerable believe this. Gabriela: And the vulnerable believe this. A lady at that age or somebody in their 50s or 60s, who are not tech savvy, immediately fall victim to these scams. V/O: Then, when Ana tried withdrawing some of the alleged profits, the scammers first demanded sixty-five thousand rand for all manner of fake charges including lost login details and a so-called “signal fee” By now, Ana had already paid more than five hundred thousand rand to the scammers, without a single pay-out in return. Finally realising she’d been scammed, she went to the Police and Standard Bank and approached Gabriela and Mikayla for help. With the assistance of all the banks involved, several suspect accounts were frozen, and the lawyers painstakingly pieced together the money trail. Mikayla: Monies were paid from Ana’s Standard Bank account into another Standard Bank account and then that money moved to Capitec to FNB and then from FNB to Tyme Bank to Capitec to Standard Bank. It just continually would move until such point that you cannot track it any more or the monies have just been withdrawn. V/O: Fryer says this is how syndicates launder money. They often have dozens of accounts, all in other people’s names. Peter: It is very common. It is typically a scenario that you would refer to as an e-mule where and individual is paid to open a legit bank account using their own FICA documentation, and once that bank account has been opened, they hand over the bank card with its pin to the syndicate members. V/O: This enables them to quickly move illicit funds around, and to withdraw cash at ATMs. To their surprise Gabriela and Mikayla found that not all the fraudulent accounts had been emptied. Link: They then filed an urgent application in the Gauteng North High Court to freeze the various accounts and have what was left in them, repaid to Mrs Viegas. V/O: They were able to recover a little over one hundred thousand rand. But who are these heartless scammers? LINK: When we looked at her Whatsapp records and the various bank accounts used to syphon off the money we identified at least 5 role players who are part of the scam. V/O: All five of these mystery individuals had contacted Ana at some stage, and we had their numbers. We tried calling them, but unsurprisingly four of them had been disconnected. Then came the fifth, belonging to a Moosa Dhlamini to whom Ana had made most of her payments. Phone ringing Moosa: Hallo. Derek: Is that Moosa? Moosa: Yes. Derek: Moosa Dlamini how are you? It is Derek Watts from Carte Blanche. We would like to talk about your involvement in an alleged scam involving Anna Viegas. Moosa: No problem. No problem. V/O: We arranged a meeting. Derek: Thanks for coming to speak to us all the way from Lens. Moosa: Thank you. I want my name to be cleared. I am not a criminal. V/O: Far from a cybercrime lynchpin, Moosa claimed to be another of the syndicate’s unsuspecting victims. His only crime? Believing in something too good to be true. Moosa: So, I was looking for something to generate income for myself and my family. So I went on Facebook, I went on Instagram, social media platforms typing in the search “How to make online money.” So I get recruited by these Falcon people. They said: Listen, we will offer you a job. We just need your services. They will send money though my account and I was to disperse the money. I was given an FNB account to transfer all the money to. Derek: That is the key. They wanted to use your account. What would you get in return? Moosa: I would get a percentage V/O: According to Moosa, he only discovered his role in the scam when his bank account was frozen after Ana reported the fraud. Derek: Did you know that Mrs Viegas was elderly and needed money to pay medical bills? Moosa: No, I had no idea. I was not permitted to know the details of the clients. V/O: Moosa claims not to have received a cent of what he was promised, and that the people who recruited him have now vanished. With one scammer’s identity known, we approached the Police for an update on Ana’s case. Their only comment was to confirm that the investigation was still ongoing. While acknowledging she was fortunate to get even some of her money back, the saga has left Ana devastated, both emotionally and financially. Derek: Really you lost half a million. Ana: That’s right. Derek: How’s that affected you? Ana: It has affected me very badly, I am living out of my old age pension. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- PROMO 11” Accepting a late-night call from a complete stranger. A promise of untold profits. A pensioner’s dream turned into a nightmare by ruthless scammers. (11) PROMO 21” ANA: If you can invest five hundred thousand, you will have one point seven million rand within two weeks. (10) A call from a complete stranger led to a loss of over half a million rand. The offer was really too good to be true. (10) PROMO 21” A WhatsApp offer on a pensioner’s cell phone was too good to ignore. (6) ANA: If you can invest five hundred thousand, you will have one point seven million rand within two weeks. (10) An opportunity if a lifetime turned into a nightmare of epic proportions. (5)

metadata.Unique Selling Point: A scam that the public should be aware of and be on the lookout for.
metadata.Summary: A group of sophisticated scammers (which includes people from law firms) are using the pretence of high profits on the Luno crypto platform to swindle people out of hundreds of thousands of rand. It is not a crypto scam at all, since no crypto currencies are actually bought as in our previous shows. Money is paid over and is then transferred to several other accounts which make it hard for even banks to recover. And then the scammers return and offer the victims a chance to get the money back – for another payment. Then they pretend they are from the Fraud Department of South Africaan o that recovers stolen money and for a percentage they claimed they can get the money back – the percentage paid up front, of course. And then they illegally withdraw money from the victims account in the night. They just do not give up!
metadata.Further information: When she was approached through a Whatsapp message to make some extra money, it was a God-send for Mrs Viegas, a 65-year old woman from Johannesburg. She suffers from chronic illnesses, including multiple sclerosis, and some extra funds could be used to address some of the most pressing needs she had. She had some savings, which was her sole source of income. She is a disability pensioner living on a very tight budget and had to be very careful with her spending. The offer of using some of her money to make a lot more was more than attractive, and she had heard of people earning fabulous amounts of money with crypto currencies. She was approached through WhatsApp by the CEO of a company referred to as Falcon Xchange, allegedly working in association with Luno, the crypto currency trading platform. She was invited to utilize an investment opportunity which could provide her with huge returns on her money, much better than any normal investment. Luno is South Africa’s biggest crypto currency platform and has an excellent track record. The people contacting her offered to create an account for her on the Falcon Xchange website and manage her portfolio. All she had to do was click on a link, fill in her details and she was set to earn substantial and quick profits on her trading account. She was advised to pay money into a Standard Bank account and paid over a total amount of R533, 850.00 She then started to receive screen shots of her growing investment account, which soon was in the range of six million rand. It all seemed very legit and the “proof” kept on coming. After a few weeks on record breaking gains, she decided to withdraw some of the profits and requested pay-outs. This never happened. Falcon Exchange started to request various fees in order for the funds to be released. These included consultation fees, registration and verification fees, signal fees, cost of transfer fees, activation fees, and so on. She insisted that they pay back her money and they sent her proof of payment from a Capitec account. The PoP was falsified and the money never arrived. Mrs Viegas quickly realised that what she believed was an investment scheme was in fact a fraudulent scam. She went to the Police and was awarded a case number. She contacted Standard Bank who attended to an internal investigation, because she initially paid the money into a Standard Bank account. Standard Bank advised that the money was transferred out of that count to a Capitec and FNB account. Mrs Viegas was advised by Standard Bank to get a court order to freeze the accounts, and for any available funds to be repatriated to her bank account. She then approached the law firm Maher Attorneys Incorporated and instructed two up and coming lawyers Mikayla Maher of Maher Attorneys Inc working in association with Gabriela Narotzky of Taitz & Skikne Attorneys. They succeed with a court application late in December 2021 to ensure the funds remained frozen and that the frozen funds or any funds recoverable from the banks would be transferred to Mrs Viegas’s account. Gabriela and Mikayla have been assisting Mrs Viegas ever since and they have determined the following: • The Standard Bank account belonged to a Mr Moosa DHlamini, a marketing intern at a reputable law firm. He received the money and paid it into an FNB and Capitec account. The court application was sent to Mr Dhlamini and to his law firm, and he has subsequently been suspended. Another account used was that of a Charmaine Ruud based at a law firm in the Eastern Cape. The attorneys have spoken to both of the these individuals and they claim they merely received money and then transferred it along to an FNB account.. • The FNB account purportedly belongs to a Mr Charles Davids. FNB has advised that there are no longer funds recoverable from this account. • The “CEO” of Falcon Xchange, who goes by the name KELVIN, (surname unknown), had his number traced on True Caller, with the number registered under the name “New Coin” – another potential cryptocurrency scam being operated by the same group. The police are investigating, and a docket has been opened. But not much more. But the saga continues! • In an unbelievable twist the same fraudsters then attempted to gain further funds from Mrs Viegas by claiming that they could refund all her money back however they would charge a fee of R10 000,00 for their assistance in claiming all her lost money back (as reflected on the Capitec Bank proof of payment). • But that was still not the end! Mrs Viegas was contacted via Whatsapp by an individual purporting to be from the Fraud Department of South Africa. The individual in question claimed that he would assist Mrs Viegas in obtaining her lost funds and would ensure she is refunded. The individual would simply require 20% of the total moneys recovered. This 20% had to be paid upfront prior to his investigation of the fraud and recoveries of the money. This was an example of yet another attempt and defrauding Mrs Viegas. • Mrs Viegas continues to receive Whatsapp messages Gabriela and Mikayla have taken Mrs Viegas under their wing and are still assisting her. The banks and Luno have been very helpful in the case, although they say as crypto is still unregulated in South Africa, there is little they can do to assist. The scam is ongoing and on one of the lawyers, Gabriela also received a Whatsapp invitation to the scam. The two lawyers say the scam in widespread and they want to bring the case to the public’s attention to warn vulnerable groups such as the elderly of the scam and how it works. Further, a new development in insurance is that there is now specialized insurance cover for instances of fraud, even in instances such as in Mrs Viegas case, where the transactions were authorised and only then found to be fraudulent. We propose that we expose the scam and confront the scammers whose whereabouts and telephone numbers are known to us. We have access to: • All Whatapp messages • Bank documents • Copies of the “investment account” • Court documents • Telephone numbers of the scammers we know of and new telephone numbers of new Whatsapp approaches. Interviewees from the following: • Mrs Viegas • Gabriela and Mikayla who worked together in association; • We have the telephone numbers of some of the scammers and the attorneys actually have had conversations with them. We can confront them. • Sean Andrews on the insurance cover available to individuals and businesses;
